items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri and the structure led by Mark Webber ended their agreement by mutual consent after seven years of relationship. Oscar Piastri has made one of the most important decisions of his sporting career: the Australian McLaren [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/mclaren]driver and the management team led by Mark Webber and his partner, Ann Webber, have agreed to end their professional relationship by mutual consent, according to a joint statement issued this Monday. News that represents a turning point in the young driver's trajectory, who, since 2019, has entrusted his career to the experience and contacts of the former Formula 1 driver. "I would like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years. Their guidance has been invaluable, especially as I navigated the start of my F1 career. I wish them all the best in the future," Piastri declared in the statement. The 25-year-old driver, currently in seventh place in the drivers' championship, faces a new stage under a renewed management structure whose details have not yet been made public. Oscar Piastri: 'Back to Where I Wanted to Be' as McLaren Struggles Ease [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/e8b2c1d7-3f6b-41b2-bd82-cc2cf0a73d37.jpeg] Oscar Piastri: 'Back to Where I Wanted to Be' as McLaren Struggles Ease The Australian admits that the start of the season was hard, but assures that the last races have been a turning point. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/oscar-piastri-back-to-where-i-wanted-to-be-as-mclaren-struggles-ease] Mark Webber, nine-time Grand Prix winner, also wanted to say goodbye with words of gratitude and pride: "We are proud to have played a fundamental role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early. After our reduced on-track involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is the right time to end our management agreement. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure and us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the best for a long and successful career," the Australian noted. Piastri's relationship with the Webbers dates back to 2019, when the young driver won his first single-seater championship with a Formula Renault Eurocup title and secured a place in Renault's Formula 1 junior program. That marked the start of a meteoric rise: the following year he became FIA Formula 3 champion, and in 2021 he repeated the title in Formula 2; his talent was evident, but his arrival in Formula 1 was not without obstacles. Alpine, the renamed Renault team, missed the chance to promote him to a full-time seat, which opened the door for McLaren to sign him. F1 2026: Updated Teammates' Head-to-Head After the Sao Paulo GP [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/c80f6a21-5816-430f-a848-568b4309ba77.jpeg] F1 2026: Updated Teammates' Head-to-Head After the Sao Paulo GP Here's a look at the updated teammate head-to-head race records after the 2026 Formula 1 São Paulo Grand Prix. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/f1-2026-updated-teammates-head-to-head-after-the-sao-paulo-gp] Mark Webber engineered that move: he negotiated with McLaren and secured an agreement for Piastri to debut in Formula 1 in 2023, replacing his compatriot Daniel Ricciardo. The decision proved a success: Piastri scored two podiums in his rookie season and, the following year, took his first Grand Prix win in Hungary. In 2025, already consolidated as one of the most promising drivers on the grid, he starred in an impressive title fight that he finally lost to his teammate, Lando Norris. This year, the Webbers had reduced their presence at the circuits, and Piastri had increasingly relied on other figures in his environment, such as his former race engineer at Prema, Pedro Matos, and his mental coach, Emma Murray. The separation, though friendly, marks a new stage in the Australian driver's career. His future at McLaren seems assured in the short term, but his new management team could open new doors for him in the driver market. Meanwhile, Piastri remains focused on his on-track performance and his objective of fighting for the title again in 2027. His talent is beyond doubt, and his decision to take the reins of his career is another step toward sporting maturity. "we are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of oscar's career. we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. Oscar Piastri, the Australian McLaren Formula 1 driver, has now parted ways with Mark Webber, the former F1 racer, and his partner Ann after almost seven years of working together.The official announcement on November 9, 2026, marked the end of their professional relationship together.Webber had played an important role in Piastri's journey from junior racing categories to the Formula 1 grid, which included his move to McLaren in 2023 also. Here’s the full story.Several social media platforms shared posts regarding the official statement featuring Mark Webber announcing the end of his management partnership with Oscar Piastri on November 9, 2026.According to the announcement, Webber, along with his partner Ann, will no longer manage the Australian driver after working with him for nearly seven years. Both have confirmed this the day after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.In the official statement, Mark expressed his pride in the pivotal role played during Oscar's formative years, mainly their contribution of getting him into competitive Formula 1 at an early stage of his career. He also highlighted his reduced trackside involvement during the 2026 season and explained that they have mutually agreed on bringing the management agreement to an end.The announcement said, “We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar’s career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early in. Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure and for us to embark on our new ventures.”Oscar Piastri also thanked Mark and Ann Webber in the same joint written statement.He said, “I’d like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years. Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.”Mark Webber and Ann had begun managing the F1 driver back in 2019, when he was still competing in junior racing categories.One of their significant contributions came up during Piastri's transition from the Alpine's junior programme to the McLaren just ahead of the 2023 season.After the departure of Fernando Alonso from Alpine, Piastri was among the drivers who were considered for a race seat, but after a contractual dispute, he then eventually secured a McLaren seat.The move was proved to be significant for his career and also allowed him to make his Formula 1 debut with McLaren in 2023.After that, the F1 driver had established himself as one of the team's leading drivers, as he recorded race victories and pole positions.He had also emerged as a championship contender during the 2025 season after spending a period at the top of the standings before he finished as third overall.Ahead of the 2026 season, during the pre-season testing in Bahrain in February 2026,Oscar had brought up additional support for his team, which included Prema Formula 2 race engineer Pedro Matos and mental coach Emma Murray. At that time he described the changes as just a practical arrangement rather than any kind of disagreement between Webber and him. Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber end their management partnership. Seven years together close. Piastri faces a new career move. Oscar Piastri has ended his management partnership with Mark Webber and Ann Webber, closing a relationship that began in 2019 and spanned his rise from junior racing to Formula One. A joint statement released on the Monday after the São Paulo Grand Prix said both sides had mutually agreed to end their management agreement. The announcement followed a tough, winless weekend for the McLaren driver, who finished sixth in São Paulo. The timing puts a personal change alongside a demanding stretch on track, but the statement offered no suggestion that the decision alters Piastri’s position with the team. For a modern F1 driver, management reaches well beyond race-weekend logistics: it can shape commercial deals, media commitments and longer-term career planning. The agreement’s end is a significant management change, but it concerns representation, not Piastri’s racing contract or his relationship with McLaren. Why Piastri and Webber’s management partnership mattered Webber, a nine-time Grand Prix winner, had guided Piastri since the Australian’s junior-category days. That long view gave the partnership a distinctive role: Webber knew the pressures of the Formula One paddock first-hand, while Piastri climbed through the ranks towards a seat at McLaren. Their collaboration also carried weight because Piastri’s route to F1 involved a high-profile dispute over his future before McLaren confirmed him for 2023. His driver management team helped steer the early stages of a career that has since put him in the fight at the front. Readers can revisit Piastri’s Formula One profile and the earlier contract story in his commitment to McLaren. A change in representation does not, by itself, signal a change in sporting direction. There is no announced replacement in the available statement, and neither side set out a reason for the decision; the confirmed fact is a mutual agreement to end the arrangement. In a sport where every move invites speculation, that distinction matters. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v88_aw4mRkqw What the management change means for Piastri’s next move Piastri now faces the practical task of deciding how to handle the commercial and off-track work previously managed by the Webbers. Whether he appoints a new representative or takes a different approach remains unannounced. For now, the partnership ending marks an administrative reset, not evidence of a wider career move. The immediate sporting focus stays with McLaren. Piastri’s results, qualifying pace and contribution to the team’s championship campaign will define his season far more than a change in driver management. His recent on-track story has included both promise and setbacks, as this report on Piastri’s impact alongside Lando Norris shows. That separation is especially important as teams and drivers plan around Formula One’s changing demands in 2026. A new representative could influence how opportunities are assessed, but it cannot alter the car’s performance or Piastri’s role in the cockpit. The measure of this decision will emerge in the choices that follow, not in assumptions about the agreement itself. Webber’s seven-year involvement ends with mutual thanks rather than a public dispute, according to the joint announcement. items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber have mutually agreed to end their management partnership. - Pitpass.com Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber have mutually agreed to end their management partnership. It was Webber who was the architect of his fellow-Australian's controversial split with Alpine, which subsequently opened the door for the back-to-back F3 and F2 champion to join McLaren. However, this year Webber has taken a step back, certainly in terms of trackside support of his driver, with Piastri's former F2 engineer appearing to fill the void, along with Emma Murray, as his psychology coach. Speaking on the High Performance podcast in May, Piastri played down the significance of Webber's absence. "When I first got into F1, Mark was coming up with questions and ideas that literally hadn't even entered my brain," he said. "I would hear him say it and go like, 'how the hell did he think of that?' or like, 'how am I ever going to think of that?' "But now, starting my fourth year, I have either the answers to a lot of those kinds of questions that I wouldn't have had in the first couple of years, or I know the questions to keep asking, which just comes with experience. "There's naturally less and less for Mark to do on the racing side of things the more experienced I become. But especially in the first couple of years, there are some lessons you have to learn the hard way, and there's no other way of doing it, but I'm sure there could have been plenty of other slightly annoying, tougher lessons to learn that I was probably spared because of Mark's experience and Mark's guidance." Maybe it is coincidence, but this year, for whatever reason, be it the new regulations, Webber's absence or whatever, Piastri has appeared a shadow of the driver we saw in 2025, when he took the title fight down to the wire. This morning Webber confirmed the end of their partnership. "We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on," said the Australian in a statement. "Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career." "I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years," added Piastri. "Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri explains how a red flag disrupted his run and led to an unexpected early exit from qualifying. Piastri rejects red-flag excuse. Tyres, not timing, decided his fate. McLaren now has a Q2 puzzle to solve. Oscar Piastri says a late red flag did not cause his unexpected qualifying exit at Interlagos. The McLaren driver finished 12th in a rain-hit session, missing the top ten by just over two tenths. His team-mate Lando Norris claimed pole with a 1m 27.470s lap, while Piastri’s best effort was 1m 30.369s. A switch from wet tyres to intermediates reshaped the battle, and Piastri believes the timing of that call mattered more than the session interruption. How the red flag affected Piastri’s qualifying exit With around 45 seconds left in Q2, Rafael Camara crashed his Haas at the final major braking zone. Race control stopped the session, denying several drivers—including Piastri—a final chance to improve. The interruption was real, but it affected the whole field rather than singling out the Australian. “Everyone would have got another lap,” Piastri said, rejecting the idea that the red flag alone explained his early exit. He acknowledged that the extra run might have helped, but pointed instead to the need to have the right tyre ready at the right moment. That distinction matters: the session interruption cut short his opportunity, but did not create the underlying grip problem. The result leaves a sharp contrast inside McLaren: Norris converted the changing conditions into pole, while Piastri could not find enough time on the intermediate tyres. The Australian’s wider season story has centred on his place in the team, including this report on his commitment to McLaren. At Interlagos, though, the immediate question was execution over a handful of laps. Tyre timing and track conditions explain the gap Piastri admitted that the team may have waited too long before moving to intermediates. He had just completed a lap, but the tyres needed another run or two to build temperature; lines that worked on the full wets no longer suited the changing surface. In mixed conditions, grip can shift faster than a driver can adapt, and the clock offers little room to recover. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vZUrgCph5IRk That left the 1m 30.369s lap short of what Q3 demanded. Piastri said there was “a lot more time” available, and suggested that another lap and better decisions could have put him through. For Formula 1 teams, the decision is not simply wet versus intermediate; it is when the tyre can deliver temperature without sacrificing a final timed attempt. There is useful context in the team-mate comparison. Norris’s 1m 27.470s pole showed how much pace the McLaren could produce, but it does not erase the changing track conditions across the session. For more on the pair’s competition, see Norris under pressure as Piastri impresses; this qualifying split was decided by timing and tyre preparation, not a simple lack of car speed. What Piastri’s early exit means for the São Paulo race Despite the disappointing grid position, Piastri said he felt comfortable with the car in the dry and that the team had a solid baseline. A dry race would give him a more predictable platform, while further rain could reopen the same tyre-temperature challenge that shaped qualifying. Either way, the race weekend is not defined by one interrupted session. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vMIAo6VJ9onQ The focus now shifts to converting that dry-weather confidence into forward progress from 12th. Piastri has not blamed luck, and his account points to a specific review for McLaren: whether the move to intermediates came late and whether the out-lap plan gave them enough time to work. The red flag closed the door on one more attempt; tyre choice had already narrowed the route to Q3. items.article_search_text: ‘Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?’ 7NEWS brings you the latest local news from Australia and around the world. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS. Australian Formula One star Oscar Piastri will start from 10th on the gird for the Sao Paulo grand prix after Lando Norris put his McLaren on pole position for the third year in a row. It was a wild Saturday (Sunday AEDT) at Interlagos in tough ‌conditions after a long delay caused by torrential rain, and extra mechanical considerations for many drivers. George Russell qualified second fastest for Mercedes, 0.204 slower, but dropped down the ‌grid due to a five-place penalty, with his newly-crowned world champion teammate Kimi Antonelli replacing him alongside last year’s race winner and champion. Ferrari’s ‌Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop due to power unit changes, which meant Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson will start third and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg fourth. “The big shock there is Oscar Piastri,” Sky Sports commentator David Croft said. “He won’t be continuing in this qualifying session”. With the rain getting heavier and leaving no chance for anyone to improve on their times in the final phase, the clock ticked down for the last five minutes without a car on track. “Today is about getting on ‌pole. It doesn’t ‌really matter how you ⁠do it, so very pleased with that,” Norris said after a qualifying that started ​and was then halted for nearly an hour and a half. Russell was furious not to be fastest, wanting to make a statement despite knowing he had a penalty but having to abort his quick lap when he came up behind Williams’ Alex Albon. “Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?,” he shouted over team radio after realising his day was done. “P2. I don’t ⁠want to be P2. I want to be P1.” Red Bull’s four-time champion ​Max Verstappen, with a 30 place grid penalty due to power unit changes, sat out the second phase that was red-flagged when Haas debutant Rafael Camara crashed. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who will also be starting at the back of the grid ​due ​to engine penalties amounting to an impossible 65 place ​drop, also went out. There was then a further delay to clear ‌debris before the decisive third phase. Conditions had eased in Q2, with double world champion Fernando Alonso leaning on his experience and the first to switch to intermediates. Camara earlier had the home crowd roaring when he reached the second phase but fellow-Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto had a nightmare for the second year running when he went off and qualified last. Bortoleto slid into the tyre wall with seven minutes to go ​but returned to the track and made his way back to the pits where the damage proved too extensive to ​fix in the time available. Both Alpines ⁠also went out at the first hurdle along with the two Cadillacs and Aston Martin’s ​Lance Stroll. Journalist from Australian news agency, Australian Associated Press.
